headline: High-risk shared filesystem and broad egress create default data-leak and cascading-error exposure; prompt-injection risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LangGraph can read/write application-defined files and has no self-isolation; transformers also reads/writes files and processes model/example inputs. If A passes untrusted content into B through shared files or stdout, B may treat it as trusted instructions. The pathway is plausible in default orchestration, though not inherently automatic.
conditions: IF agent_a writes attacker-controlled text into a file that agent_b later parses as instructions
IF the two agents share a workspace or stdout/stderr bridge without provenance tagging
mitigations: Separate workspaces for A and B
Prefix all inter-agent payloads with a strict schema marker
Reject instruction-like text from B unless signed by A
Disable automatic parsing of free-form file contents
requires-engineering: add provenance tracking to the handoff layer

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress and filesystem access, and A explicitly handles model provider API keys while B touches multimodal data. In a shared workspace, either can read the other's files and exfiltrate sensitive contents to external services by default. The blast radius includes secrets and user data, so this is high.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share any writable directory
IF either agent is allowed to send file contents to external APIs or hubs
mitigations: Use separate OS users and directories
Mount sensitive inputs read-only
Block outbound network for the agent that should not exfiltrate
Store secrets outside shared workspaces
requires-engineering: add DLP filtering on inter-agent file transfers

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem, execute shells, spawn subprocesses, and use broad network egress. LangGraph also supports multiple instances via a shared checkpointer store, while transformers can run multiple instances too. Without explicit locking, concurrent writes to shared files or state can corrupt outputs or overwrite each other's work.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory or checkpointer-backed state
IF no external lock or transaction boundary serializes writes
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Use file locks around shared artifacts
Serialize write phases in the orchestrator
Make one agent read-only
requires-engineering: add transactional state coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph is an orchestration framework that can emit state or tool outputs, and transformers commonly consumes files or scripts as pipeline inputs. If B treats A's output as authoritative without verification, errors or hallucinated facts can propagate into downstream processing. The pair does not inherently force this, but the default handoff pattern makes it plausible.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a outputs without validation
IF A-generated state is used as input to B's pipeline or scripts
mitigations: Insert a validation step between A and B
Require schema checks on A's outputs
Have B re-derive critical facts from source data
Log and diff A outputs before downstream use
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks

E_compliance.rationale: A touches graph state and model provider API keys, while B processes multimodal data and can call Hugging Face Hub or transformers serve. The profiles do not specify residency or retention controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible if regulated data flows through the pair. Uncertainty pushes this above low because the data classes and external calls are broad.
conditions: IF regulated personal data is processed through either agent
IF retention or residency requirements differ between the two deployment environments
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair
Document retention settings for both agents
Disable external API calls for regulated workloads
Review data residency before deployment
requires-engineering: implement policy-based routing and retention controls
